Beyond leading asymptotics in the lattice nonlinear Schrödinger model

Trans-series, boundary reconstruction, and spectral determinants

A continuation of arXiv:2603.09522v3

Istvan Vona

12 November 2026

Download PDFLaTeX source ZIP Paper + code + data

Abstract

The weak-coupling lattice nonlinear Schrödinger equation is a Love integral equation with a Lorentzian source. Its density, central rapidity distribution, and energy are point-resolvent observables rather than polynomial moments. Starting from the September 2026 analysis of Sant’Ana, we develop their beyond-all-orders description and several exact extensions. A commuting-flow representation supplies a formal endpoint seed, and first-order ordinary differential equations reduce the remaining endpoint functions to triangular recursions. A finite matrix path expansion then generates every formal sector in Λ=exp⁡(−2⁢π⁢Q)\Lambda=\exp(-2\pi Q). We generate approximately 200 coefficients per sector and compare lateral Borel–Leroy–Padé sums with independent integral-equation solutions: the density and central-density sectors are resolved through Λ7\Lambda^{7}, while their eighth sectors remain unstable. Exact interval-variation identities determine the Fredholm determinant from the constant-source boundary value. They enforce an even-sector selection rule, yield an analytic Fisher–Hartwig normalization, and permit numerical resolution of its Λ8\Lambda^{8} contribution. Separately, we prove a convergent boundary-to-bulk reconstruction and a regularized spectral-determinant scaling limit governed by the restricted half-Laplacian, including an explicit inverse-square spectral sum. We derive and test grand-canonical and fixed-density T4T^{4} coefficients. Exact identities, formal resurgent constructions, and numerical evidence are distinguished throughout: a global Borel-reconstruction theorem and exponentially small corrections to individual eigenvalues are not claimed. Code, coefficients, parameter scans, and interval-certified reference values accompany the manuscript.

Keywords: lattice nonlinear Schrödinger model; Love integral equation; resurgence; Wiener–Hopf factorization; Fredholm determinants; fractional Laplacian.

Data and proof status. The supplementary archive contains executable tests and all plotted data. The endpoint spectral-contour step is a formal construction, not a uniform analytic Borel theorem. The supplied commuting-flow note by Dániel Nógrádi is cited as unpublished material.

1 Introduction and scope#

The quantum lattice nonlinear Schrödinger model, equivalently the isotropic negative-spin chain at s=−1s=-1, provides an integrable setting in which weak coupling leads to a singular Fredholm problem. Sant’Ana’s September revision [1] resolves its inner, bulk, and edge regions by identifying the kernel with the Cauchy transition density. The central logarithm, the density constant, the Love-equation duality, and the leading restricted-half-Laplacian eigenvalue scaling are already established there. The same analysis identifies exp⁡(−2⁢π⁢Q)\exp(-2\pi Q) as a candidate beyond-all-orders scale, while explicitly distinguishing that observation from a derivation of Borel singularities and Stokes data.

The present work starts at that distinction. Locating a zero of a Wiener–Hopf symbol does not determine which sectors occur in a given observable, their coefficients, or the prescription that reconstructs a real finite-interval solution. The difficulty is especially visible here: a point evaluation of a resolvent is not one of the polynomial moments for which a complete trans-series framework is available [2, 3, 4]. We construct the additional endpoint functions, reduce them to differential recursions, and test the resulting sectors without fitting them to the integral-equation data.

The classical Love problem [5] and its relation to the Lieb–Liniger gas [6] have a substantial analytical literature; Farina, Lang, and Martin provide a broad review [7]. High-order bulk–edge matching follows the method of Volin [8, 9], developed for weakly coupled gases by Mariño and Reis [10] and for the circular capacitor by Reichert and Ristivojevic [11]. The resurgent extensions and running-coupling conventions used below come from the Bajnok framework [12, 13, 2]. An unpublished commuting-flow note supplied with the source material [14] gives a more efficient representation of the perturbative input. We explicitly distinguish that input from the endpoint extension proposed here.

There is a complementary exact structure. Interval differentiation of a convolution resolvent produces rank-two boundary terms. These identities connect the boundary value, the determinant, and a hyperbolic boundary-to-bulk equation. This is related in spirit to the general resolvent and canonical-system constructions of Refs. [15, 16]; we do not claim that interval variation as a method is new. Its specialization here gives a particularly economical reconstruction of all lattice observables.

1.1 What is inherited and what is added#

The manuscript uses version 3 of Ref. [1], dated 4 September 2026, rather than the March text. This matters for attribution. In particular, neither the density constant nor the leading 1/Q1/Q operator gap is an unresolved question in that revision. Likewise, the finite-temperature TBA and the gapless low-energy interpretation are already treated by Zhong et al. [17]. Our thermodynamic contribution is the reduction of higher low-temperature coefficients to the same endpoint data, together with their numerical tests.

The term all-sector construction is used in a precise algorithmic sense: at a prescribed exponential order and a prescribed power of the running coupling, only finitely many differential recursions and matrix products are required. It does not assert convergence of the infinite sector sum, a uniform error estimate, or a proof that the chosen lateral completion equals the exact solution for all positive QQ.

1.2 Normalized equation and physical limits#

On [−Q,Q][-Q,Q] define

KQ⁢(x,y)=K⁢(x−y),K⁢(x)=1π⁢(1+x2).K_{Q}(x,y)=K(x-y),\qquad K(x)=\frac{1}{\pi(1+x^{2})}. (1.1)

The two basic equations are

(I−KQ)⁢fQ=1,(I−KQ)⁢ρQ=K.(I-K_{Q})f_{Q}=1,\qquad(I-K_{Q})\rho_{Q}=K. (1.2)

The notation KQK_{Q} denotes both the integral operator and its kernel. The lattice density, central value, and dimensionless energy are

D⁢(Q)=∫−QQρQ⁢(x)⁢dx=fQ⁢(0)−1,R⁢(Q)=ρQ⁢(0),E⁢(Q)=2⁢π⁢R⁢(Q)−2.D(Q)=\int_{-Q}^{Q}\rho_{Q}(x)\mathrm{d}x=f_{Q}(0)-1,\qquad R(Q)=\rho_{Q}(0),% \qquad E(Q)=2\pi R(Q)-2. (1.3)

We write RR for the scalar central value and ℛQ\mathscr{R}_{Q} for the resolvent kernel, to avoid confusing them. Self-adjointness proves the density identity directly. Indeed, K=KQ⁢δ0K=K_{Q}\delta_{0}, so

ρQ⁢(x)=ℛQ⁢(x,0),ℛQ=KQ⁢(I−KQ)−1=(I−KQ)−1−I.\rho_{Q}(x)=\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,0),\qquad\mathscr{R}_{Q}=K_{Q}(I-K_{Q})^{-1}=(I-% K_{Q})^{-1}-I. (1.4)

For every finite QQ,

‖KQ‖∞→∞=2π⁢arctan⁡Q<1,\|K_{Q}\|_{\infty\to\infty}=\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan Q<1, (1.5)

which proves existence, uniqueness, and positivity of the solutions.

The original coupling and Fermi rapidity obey

Q=qκ,ρ~⁢(x)=κ⁢ρphysical⁢(κ⁢x),e⁢(κ,q)=−1κ⁢E⁢(q/κ).Q=\frac{q}{\kappa},\qquad\widetilde{\rho}(x)=\kappa\rho_{\rm physical}(\kappa x% ),\qquad e(\kappa,q)=-\frac{1}{\kappa}E(q/\kappa). (1.6)

Thus Q→∞Q\to\infty is weak coupling at fixed qq, or a high-filling limit. At fixed finite density, D=D⁢(Q)D=D(Q) instead fixes QQ and gives q=κ⁢Qq=\kappa Q; it does not produce an additional large-QQ limit. The energy sign and the factor 1/κ1/\kappa are kept separate from the positive function EE throughout.

The inherited leading terms are

D⁢(Q)\displaystyle D(Q) =Q+log⁡Q2⁢π+1+log⁡(16⁢π)2⁢π−1+o⁢(1),\displaystyle=Q+\frac{\log Q}{2\pi}+\frac{1+\log(16\pi)}{2\pi}-1+o(1), (1.7)
R⁢(Q)\displaystyle R(Q) =log⁡(2⁢Q)+γEπ+o⁢(1).\displaystyle=\frac{\log(2Q)+\gamma_{E}}{\pi}+o(1). (1.8)

They will fix integration constants, not be refitted in numerical comparisons.

1.3 Running-coupling dictionary#

The resurgent calculation uses

b=π⁢Q,2⁢b=1v+log⁡v8⁢e,Λ=e−2⁢b=8⁢ev⁢e−1/v,0<v<1,b=\pi Q,\qquad 2b=\frac{1}{v}+\log\frac{v}{8e},\qquad\Lambda=e^{-2b}=\frac{8e}% {v}e^{-1/v},\qquad 0<v<1, (1.9)

where the small-vv branch is selected. Dots denote bb-derivatives:

F˙=−2⁢v21−v⁢∂vF.\dot{F}=-\frac{2v^{2}}{1-v}\partial_{v}F. (1.10)

In exact Fredholm and thermodynamic formulas, primes denote QQ-derivatives unless explicitly stated otherwise. The constant-source function of Ref. [2] is 2⁢fQ2f_{Q}. Its rapidity variable is θ=π⁢x\theta=\pi x, with endpoint bb; its kernel is [(θ−θ′)2+π2]−1[(\theta-\theta^{\prime})^{2}+\pi^{2}]^{-1}.

The supplied O(3) note [14] uses an auxiliary variable ss and flow coordinate xflx_{\rm fl}. The correct dictionary is

s=v,xfl=b+32⁢log⁡2.s=v,\qquad x_{\rm fl}=b+\frac{3}{2}\log 2. (1.11)

Its physical O(3) coupling gg is not vv; g∼2⁢vg\sim 2v. The raw ne,nrn_{e},n_{r} coefficient file and the note’s physical-coupling table provide separate checks of this distinction. Applying an additional coupling transformation and identifying its output with vv would change the seed incorrectly.

2 Exact boundary control of the finite-interval problem#

Define the constant-source boundary value and the lattice boundary density by

χ⁢(Q)=fQ⁢(Q),η⁢(Q)=ρQ⁢(Q).\chi(Q)=f_{Q}(Q),\qquad\eta(Q)=\rho_{Q}(Q). (2.1)

The identities in this section hold for every finite positive QQ. They do not require the trans-series construction of section 3. They also explain why the exact point observables contain no independent functional datum once χ\chi is known on the whole interval of endpoint lengths.

2.1 Interval variation and the determinant#

Let

r⁢(Q)=ℛQ⁢(Q,Q),s⁢(Q)=ℛQ⁢(Q,−Q),𝒢⁢(Q)=log⁢det(I−KQ).r(Q)=\mathscr{R}_{Q}(Q,Q),\qquad s(Q)=\mathscr{R}_{Q}(Q,-Q),\qquad\mathcal{G}(% Q)=\log\det(I-K_{Q}). (2.2)

Domain differentiation and an integration by parts in the convolution resolvent equation give

∂QℛQ⁢(x,y)\displaystyle\partial_{Q}\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,y) =ℛQ⁢(x,Q)⁢ℛQ⁢(Q,y)+ℛQ⁢(x,−Q)⁢ℛQ⁢(−Q,y),\displaystyle=\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,Q)\mathscr{R}_{Q}(Q,y)+\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,-Q)% \mathscr{R}_{Q}(-Q,y), (2.3)
(∂x+∂y)⁢ℛQ⁢(x,y)\displaystyle(\partial_{x}+\partial_{y})\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,y) =ℛQ⁢(x,−Q)⁢ℛQ⁢(−Q,y)−ℛQ⁢(x,Q)⁢ℛQ⁢(Q,y).\displaystyle=\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,-Q)\mathscr{R}_{Q}(-Q,y)-\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,Q)% \mathscr{R}_{Q}(Q,y). (2.4)

These are the finite-rank boundary terms familiar in Fredholm differential identities [15]. Here they immediately imply

r′=2⁢s2,χ′=2⁢s⁢χ,𝒢′=−2⁢r.r^{\prime}=2s^{2},\qquad\chi^{\prime}=2s\chi,\qquad\mathcal{G}^{\prime}=-2r. (2.5)

For example, the total derivative of ℛQ⁢(Q,Q)\mathscr{R}_{Q}(Q,Q) includes both spatial derivatives; combining equations (2.3) and (2.4) cancels r2r^{2} and leaves 2⁢s22s^{2}. Similarly,

∂QfQ⁢(x)\displaystyle\partial_{Q}f_{Q}(x) =χ⁢[ℛQ⁢(x,Q)+ℛQ⁢(x,−Q)],\displaystyle=\chi\,[\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,Q)+\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,-Q)], (2.6)
∂xfQ⁢(x)\displaystyle\partial_{x}f_{Q}(x) =χ⁢[ℛQ⁢(x,−Q)−ℛQ⁢(x,Q)]\displaystyle=\chi\,[\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,-Q)-\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,Q)] (2.7)

give χ′=2⁢s⁢χ\chi^{\prime}=2s\chi at the moving endpoint.

Proposition 2.1 (Boundary formula for the determinant).

For the normalized Love operator,

𝒢′′⁢(Q)=−[∂Qlog⁡χ⁢(Q)]2,\mathcal{G}^{\prime\prime}(Q)=-\left[\partial_{Q}\log\chi(Q)\right]^{2}, (2.8)

and

𝒢⁢(Q)=−2⁢Qπ−∫0Q(Q−u)⁢[∂ulog⁡χ⁢(u)]2⁢du.\mathcal{G}(Q)=-\frac{2Q}{\pi}-\int_{0}^{Q}(Q-u)[\partial_{u}\log\chi(u)]^{2}% \mathrm{d}u. (2.9)
Proof.

The differential identity follows from equation (2.5). At zero interval length, χ⁢(0)=1\chi(0)=1, 𝒢⁢(0)=0\mathcal{G}(0)=0, and 𝒢′⁢(0)=−2⁢K⁢(0)=−2/π\mathcal{G}^{\prime}(0)=-2K(0)=-2/\pi. Twice integrating fixes both constants and gives equation (2.9). ∎

The parity decomposition gives a useful independent normalization test. On [0,Q][0,Q], let F±F_{\pm} be the determinants with kernels K⁢(x−y)±K⁢(x+y)K(x-y)\pm K(x+y). Then

F=F+⁢F−,χ=F−F+.F=F_{+}F_{-},\qquad\chi=\frac{F_{-}}{F_{+}}. (2.10)

Indeed, (log⁡F±)′=−(r±s)(\log F_{\pm})^{\prime}=-(r\pm s) and both determinants equal one at Q=0Q=0.

The central observables obey the equally simple identities

D′=2⁢χ⁢η,R′=2⁢η2,D^{\prime}=2\chi\eta,\qquad R^{\prime}=2\eta^{2}, (2.11)

so that

R′=12⁢(D′χ)2.R^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{D^{\prime}}{\chi}\right)^{2}. (2.12)

In the bb-coordinate the last formula is

R˙=π2⁢(D˙χ)2.\dot{R}=\frac{\pi}{2}\left(\frac{\dot{D}}{\chi}\right)^{2}. (2.13)

The factor of π\pi is essential when passing between the exact and formal calculations.

2.2 A convergent boundary-to-bulk reconstruction#

The complete profile satisfies a hyperbolic equation.

Theorem 2.2 (Boundary reconstruction).

For |x|<Q|x|<Q,

∂Q2fQ⁢(x)−∂x2fQ⁢(x)=2⁢χ′⁢(Q)χ⁢(Q)⁢∂QfQ⁢(x).\partial_{Q}^{2}f_{Q}(x)-\partial_{x}^{2}f_{Q}(x)=2\frac{\chi^{\prime}(Q)}{% \chi(Q)}\partial_{Q}f_{Q}(x). (2.14)

Let a=χ′/χa=\chi^{\prime}/\chi, V=a2−a′V=a^{2}-a^{\prime}, and fQ⁢(x)=χ⁢(Q)⁢ψ⁢(Q,x)f_{Q}(x)=\chi(Q)\psi(Q,x). In characteristic variables ξ=Q+x\xi=Q+x, ζ=Q−x\zeta=Q-x, the unique solution is given by the convergent integral equation

ψ⁢(ξ,ζ)=1+14⁢∫0ξds⁢∫0ζdt⁢V⁢(s+t2)⁢ψ⁢(s,t).\psi(\xi,\zeta)=1+\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{\xi}\mathrm{d}s\int_{0}^{\zeta}\mathrm{% d}t\,V\!\left(\frac{s+t}{2}\right)\psi(s,t). (2.15)

Consequently,

D⁢(Q)+1=χ⁢(Q)⁢ψ⁢(Q,Q).D(Q)+1=\chi(Q)\psi(Q,Q). (2.16)
Proof.

Write R±⁢(x,Q)=ℛQ⁢(x,±Q)R_{\pm}(x,Q)=\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,\pm Q). Combining interval and translation differentiation yields

∂QR+=−∂xR++2⁢s⁢R−,∂QR−=∂xR−+2⁢s⁢R+.\partial_{Q}R_{+}=-\partial_{x}R_{+}+2sR_{-},\qquad\partial_{Q}R_{-}=\partial_% {x}R_{-}+2sR_{+}. (2.17)

Differentiate equations (2.6) and (2.7), use χ′=2⁢s⁢χ\chi^{\prime}=2s\chi, and eliminate R±R_{\pm}. This proves equation (2.14). Substitution of f=χ⁢ψf=\chi\psi gives

ψξ⁢ζ=14⁢V⁢((ξ+ζ)/2)⁢ψ.\psi_{\xi\zeta}=\tfrac{1}{4}V((\xi+\zeta)/2)\psi. (2.18)

The endpoint values fQ⁢(±Q)=χ⁢(Q)f_{Q}(\pm Q)=\chi(Q) imply ψ⁢(ξ,0)=ψ⁢(0,ζ)=1\psi(\xi,0)=\psi(0,\zeta)=1. Integrating twice gives equation (2.15).

On a finite rectangle where |V|≤M|V|\leq M, the nnth iterate of its integral operator, applied to one, has absolute value at most

(M⁢ξ⁢ζ/4)n(n!)2.\frac{(M\xi\zeta/4)^{n}}{(n!)^{2}}. (2.19)

The corresponding majorant converges uniformly. The same iteration applied to the difference of two solutions proves uniqueness. Evaluation at x=0x=0 gives equation (2.16). ∎

This is an exact version of the boundary-to-interior philosophy in convolution and canonical-system theory [16]. In particular, it is not an asymptotic inverse problem requiring a second arbitrary integration function. For two potentials bounded by MM whose uniform difference is δ\delta, the difference of their Volterra iterates is bounded by

δ⁢∑n≥1n⁢Mn−1⁢(ξ⁢ζ/4)n(n!)2,\delta\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{nM^{n-1}(\xi\zeta/4)^{n}}{(n!)^{2}}, (2.20)

which also supplies finite-interval stability.

The central density and full lattice profile can then be recovered without another Fredholm inversion:

R⁢(Q)\displaystyle R(Q) =1π+12⁢∫0Q(D′⁢(s)χ⁢(s))2⁢ds,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\pi}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{Q}\left(\frac{D^{\prime}(s)}{% \chi(s)}\right)^{2}\mathrm{d}s, (2.21)
ρQ⁢(x)\displaystyle\rho_{Q}(x) =η⁢(|x|)+∫|x|Qη⁢(s)χ⁢(s)⁢∂sfs⁢(x)⁢d⁢s,η=D′2⁢χ.\displaystyle=\eta(|x|)+\int_{|x|}^{Q}\frac{\eta(s)}{\chi(s)}\partial_{s}f_{s}% (x)\mathrm{d}s,\qquad\eta=\frac{D^{\prime}}{2\chi}. (2.22)

For equation (2.22), vary the interval in ℛQ⁢(x,0)\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,0) and use equation (2.6); at Q=|x|Q=|x| the value is η⁢(|x|)\eta(|x|). The initial central value is R⁢(0)=K⁢(0)=1/πR(0)=K(0)=1/\pi.

Remark 2.3 (Exact information versus asymptotic seeds).

The exact function χ\chi on 0≤s≤Q0\leq s\leq Q determines the observables. A formal expansion of χ\chi at Q=∞Q=\infty is not that function on the entire integration range. Inserting a divergent large-QQ series into equation (2.15) down to Q=0Q=0 would be invalid. The two perturbative seeds used below are therefore an algorithmic choice, not two independent exact solutions. The reconstruction supplies a route to proving their compatibility, but does not itself justify the endpoint Borel contour.

For orientation, the Q=0.9Q=0.9 reconstruction at grid size 256256 gives D=0.8146009425241081D=0.8146009425241081, compared with 0.81460094252788799⁢…0.81460094252788799\ldots from the independent Fredholm solve. At Q=2Q=2, size 512512 gives 1.9706948383773161.970694838377316 instead of 1.97069483838877704⁢…1.97069483838877704\ldots. All grid sizes, including the finest-grid loss of clean Richardson scaling at Q=0.9Q=0.9, are retained in figure 1 and the supplementary data.

3 An all-sector formal construction for the point observables#

This section gives a finite algorithm for every coefficient of DD, RR, and EE. Its input is the fixed-source Wiener–Hopf basis of Ref. [2] and the commuting flows of Ref. [14]. The endpoint extension is a formal construction, supported below by exact low-order checks and high-precision comparisons. We do not promote its nonuniform spectral-contour step to a theorem about Borel sums.

3.1 Why ordinary moments are not enough#

Let χα⁢(θ)\chi_{\alpha}(\theta) solve the rescaled equation with source cosh⁡(α⁢θ)\cosh(\alpha\theta), and define

Oα⁢β⁢(b)=12⁢π⁢∫−bbcosh⁡(β⁢θ)⁢χα⁢(θ)⁢dθ=Oβ⁢α⁢(b).O_{\alpha\beta}(b)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-b}^{b}\cosh(\beta\theta)\chi_{\alpha}(% \theta)\mathrm{d}\theta=O_{\beta\alpha}(b). (3.1)

At finite bb, analytic continuation to imaginary source labels is unambiguous. The identity

πθ2+π2=∫0∞e−π⁢s⁢cos⁡(s⁢θ)⁢ds\frac{\pi}{\theta^{2}+\pi^{2}}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\pi s}\cos(s\theta)\mathrm% {d}s (3.2)

then proves the exact transforms

D⁢(Q)\displaystyle D(Q) =2⁢∫0∞e−π⁢s⁢O0,i⁢s⁢(b)⁢ds,\displaystyle=2\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\pi s}O_{0,is}(b)\mathrm{d}s, (3.3)
R⁢(Q)\displaystyle R(Q) =1π+2⁢∫0∞∫0∞e−π⁢(s+t)⁢Oi⁢s,i⁢t⁢(b)⁢ds⁢dt.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\pi}+2\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\pi(s+t)}% O_{is,it}(b)\mathrm{d}s\mathrm{d}t. (3.4)

These identities relate the lattice observables to the moment framework. They do not justify termwise use of the large-bb expansion near s=t=0s=t=0: that source limit is nonuniform. A direct imaginary-source expansion would obscure the logarithmic terms and the external residues.

The perturbative fixed-source functions satisfy [3, 2]

A˙α⁢β+(α+β)⁢Aα⁢β=aα⁢aβ,a¨α+2⁢α⁢a˙α=U⁢aα,U=a¨0a0.\dot{A}_{\alpha\beta}+(\alpha+\beta)A_{\alpha\beta}=a_{\alpha}a_{\beta},\qquad% \ddot{a}_{\alpha}+2\alpha\dot{a}_{\alpha}=Ua_{\alpha},\qquad U=\frac{\ddot{a}_% {0}}{a_{0}}. (3.5)

The constant-source seed obeys A˙00=a02\dot{A}_{00}=a_{0}^{2}. Define the endpoint transform of the perturbative basis, with the same lateral contour convention as its Wiener–Hopf factors, by

Iα=∫0∞e−π⁢s⁢[G+⁢(−s)⁢ei⁢s⁢b⁢Aα,i⁢s+G−⁢(−s)⁢e−i⁢s⁢b⁢Aα,−i⁢s]⁢ds.I_{\alpha}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\pi s}\left[G_{+}(-s)e^{isb}A_{\alpha,is}+G_{-% }(-s)e^{-isb}A_{\alpha,-is}\right]\mathrm{d}s. (3.6)

The perturbative endpoint contribution satisfies I0=π⁢D0I_{0}=\pi D_{0}. Differentiating the phases as well as the basis in equation (3.6) cancels the source label:

I˙α+α⁢Iα=aα⁢h,h=I˙0a0.\dot{I}_{\alpha}+\alpha I_{\alpha}=a_{\alpha}h,\qquad h=\frac{\dot{I}_{0}}{a_{% 0}}. (3.7)

Once hh is known, no source integration is required. The equation at α=0\alpha=0 is an identity, however; it does not generate I0I_{0} from A00A_{00}. This is the missing perturbative datum that the flow extension supplies.

3.2 Separating the zero-time seed from odd zeta values#

We first summarize the supplied flow representation [14]. Set

t=1−2⁢w,∂xfl=−2⁢w2t⁢∂w,w=v+12⁢v3+34⁢v4+⋯.t=\sqrt{1-2w},\qquad\partial_{x_{\rm fl}}=-\frac{2w^{2}}{t}\partial_{w},\qquad w% =v+\frac{1}{2}v^{3}+\frac{3}{4}v^{4}+\cdots. (3.8)

The zero-time potential and amplitude are

U∗=−w2⁢(1+w2)(1−2⁢w)3,a0,∗=12⁢tw.U_{*}=-\frac{w^{2}(1+w^{2})}{(1-2w)^{3}},\qquad a_{0,*}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac% {t}{w}}. (3.9)

Let L=∂xfl2−UL=\partial_{x_{\rm fl}}^{2}-U. The Lenard polynomials are fixed by

G0=−12,Gj+1′=(∂xfl3−4⁢U⁢∂xfl−2⁢U′)⁢Gj,G_{0}=-\frac{1}{2},\qquad G_{j+1}^{\prime}=(\partial_{x_{\rm fl}}^{3}-4U% \partial_{x_{\rm fl}}-2U^{\prime})G_{j}, (3.10)

with primitives zero at w=0w=0. Primes in equations (3.10), (3.18) and (3.19) mean xflx_{\rm fl}-derivatives, which are identical to bb-derivatives. The times are

τ2⁢j+1=−4j−1(2⁢j+1)⁢16j⁢ζ⁢(2⁢j+1),j≥1.\tau_{2j+1}=-\frac{4^{j}-1}{(2j+1)16^{j}}\zeta(2j+1),\qquad j\geq 1. (3.11)

Their action on the potential and zero-source amplitude is

∂τ2⁢j+1U=−Gj+1′,∂τ2⁢j+1a0=(2⁢Gj⁢∂xfl−Gj′)⁢a0.\partial_{\tau_{2j+1}}U=-G_{j+1}^{\prime},\qquad\partial_{\tau_{2j+1}}a_{0}=(2% G_{j}\partial_{x_{\rm fl}}-G_{j}^{\prime})a_{0}. (3.12)

The practical advantage is that one retains the flow structure rather than expanding very large polynomials of independent odd-zeta monomials at each matching step.

The endpoint seed requires the even part of the normalized spectral multiplier

m⁢(k)=π⁢ 2−k⁢Γ⁢(1+k/2)Γ⁢((1+k)/2).m(k)=\sqrt{\pi}\,2^{-k}\frac{\Gamma(1+k/2)}{\Gamma((1+k)/2)}. (3.13)

The reflection identities for Γ\Gamma give

m⁢(k)⁢m⁢(−k)=ℰ⁢(k2),ℰ⁢(z)=π⁢z2⁢cot⁡π⁢z2,ℰ⁢(0)=1.\sqrt{m(k)m(-k)}=\mathcal{E}(k^{2}),\qquad\mathcal{E}(z)=\sqrt{\frac{\pi\sqrt{% z}}{2}\cot\frac{\pi\sqrt{z}}{2}},\quad\mathcal{E}(0)=1. (3.14)

The odd logarithm is

log⁡m⁢(k)−log⁡m⁢(−k)2=−∑j≥14j⁢τ2⁢j+1⁢k2⁢j+1.\frac{\log m(k)-\log m(-k)}{2}=-\sum_{j\geq 1}4^{j}\tau_{2j+1}k^{2j+1}. (3.15)

Thus the even-zeta contribution belongs to the initial endpoint function, while the odd-zeta dependence is supplied by the times. Double-counting either part changes the perturbative coefficients.

Formal construction 3.1 (Endpoint seed and flow).

Use the zero-time function

h∗=ℰ⁢(L∗)⁢2⁢wt3/2,L∗=∂xfl2−U∗.h_{*}=\mathcal{E}(L_{*})\frac{2\sqrt{w}}{t^{3/2}},\qquad L_{*}=\partial_{x_{% \rm fl}}^{2}-U_{*}. (3.16)

The operator is expanded at zero,

ℰ⁢(L)=1−π224⁢L−π4640⁢L2+⋯,\mathcal{E}(L)=1-\frac{\pi^{2}}{24}L-\frac{\pi^{4}}{640}L^{2}+\cdots, (3.17)

so every coefficient requires only finitely many differentiations. Evolve hh by

Pj\displaystyle P_{j} =∑i=0j4j−i⁢(2⁢Gi⁢∂xfl−Gi′)⁢Lj−i,\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{j}4^{j-i}(2G_{i}\partial_{x_{\rm fl}}-G_{i}^{\prime}% )L^{j-i}, (3.18)
∂τ2⁢j+1h\displaystyle\partial_{\tau_{2j+1}}h =Pj⁢h,\displaystyle=P_{j}h, (3.19)

where the powers of LL act first. Integrate

A˙00=a02,D˙0=a0⁢hπ,R˙0=h22⁢π.\dot{A}_{00}=a_{0}^{2},\qquad\dot{D}_{0}=\frac{a_{0}h}{\pi},\qquad\dot{R}_{0}=% \frac{h^{2}}{2\pi}. (3.20)

The integration constants are fixed by the leading Love asymptotics in equation (1.7) and by

A00=116⁢v2−14⁢v−116+O⁢(v),R0=−log⁡(π⁢v)+γEπ+O⁢(v).A_{00}=\frac{1}{16v^{2}}-\frac{1}{4v}-\frac{1}{16}+O(v),\qquad R_{0}=\frac{-% \log(\pi v)+\gamma_{E}}{\pi}+O(v). (3.21)

For example, P1=−4⁢∂3+6⁢U⁢∂+3⁢U′P_{1}=-4\partial^{3}+6U\partial+3U^{\prime}. Since L⁢a0=0La_{0}=0, the general differential operator reduces on a0a_{0} to the simpler flow in the supplied note. It does not reduce in that way on hh. This is why the endpoint extension requires the full ordered operator.

The formal spectral calculation leading to equation (3.16) is recorded in appendix A. It combines the central contribution in the zero-time inversion with equation (3.14). The decomposition of the multiplier is exact, but the inversion and separation from endpoint-exponentially-small contributions have not been controlled uniformly. Consequently, formal construction 3.1 is not stated as a global analytic theorem. It is testable coefficient by coefficient and by its complete nonperturbative predictions.

3.4 Reduction to first-order coefficient recursions#

For positive integers r,sr,s, write

ar=a−2⁢r,Xr=A0,−2⁢r,Nr⁢s=A−2⁢r,−2⁢s,Ir=I−2⁢r.a_{r}=a_{-2r},\quad X_{r}=A_{0,-2r},\quad N_{rs}=A_{-2r,-2s},\quad I_{r}=I_{-2% r}. (3.26)

They satisfy

a¨r−4⁢r⁢a˙r\displaystyle\ddot{a}_{r}-4r\dot{a}_{r} =U⁢ar,ar=1+O⁢(v),\displaystyle=Ua_{r},\qquad a_{r}=1+O(v), (3.27)
X˙r−2⁢r⁢Xr\displaystyle\dot{X}_{r}-2rX_{r} =a0⁢ar,\displaystyle=a_{0}a_{r}, (3.28)
N˙r⁢s−2⁢(r+s)⁢Nr⁢s\displaystyle\dot{N}_{rs}-2(r+s)N_{rs} =ar⁢as,\displaystyle=a_{r}a_{s}, (3.29)
I˙r−2⁢r⁢Ir\displaystyle\dot{I}_{r}-2rI_{r} =ar⁢h.\displaystyle=a_{r}h. (3.30)

For a first-order equation F˙+λ⁢F=H\dot{F}+\lambda F=H, with F=vμ⁢∑fn⁢vnF=v^{\mu}\sum f_{n}v^{n} and H=vμ⁢∑hn⁢vnH=v^{\mu}\sum h_{n}v^{n}, the recursion is

fn=1λ⁢[hn+2⁢∑k=0n−1(μ+k)⁢fk].f_{n}=\frac{1}{\lambda}\left[h_{n}+2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(\mu+k)f_{k}\right]. (3.31)

Maintaining the partial sum makes this inversion linear in the number of coefficients. The second-order equation equation (3.27) is triangular as well; the first nonzero term containing the new coefficient comes from the drift term. Homogeneous solutions growing as e2⁢r⁢be^{2rb} are excluded by the prescribed formal power series. For fixed maximum sector, the expensive step is generating the scalar flow seeds; it is not the endpoint ODE inversion.

3.5 Complete internal, external, and mixed sectors#

In the upper-lateral convention define

Cr=(r/e)r(r−1)!⁢2⁢π⁢r,S2⁢r=2⁢i⁢(r/e)2⁢r(r−1)!⁢r!=4⁢π⁢i⁢Cr2.C_{r}=\frac{(r/e)^{r}}{(r-1)!\sqrt{2\pi r}},\qquad S_{2r}=\frac{2\mathrm{i}(r/% e)^{2r}}{(r-1)!r!}=4\pi\mathrm{i}C_{r}^{2}. (3.32)

The S2⁢rS_{2r} are the fixed-source Stokes factors of Ref. [2]. Let

Pr⁢s=δr⁢s⁢S2⁢r⁢Λ2⁢r,cr=4⁢π⁢i⁢Cr⁢Λr,P_{rs}=\delta_{rs}S_{2r}\Lambda^{2r},\qquad c_{r}=4\pi\mathrm{i}C_{r}\Lambda^{% r}, (3.33)

where cc is the vector of external source residues. Set

M=(1−P⁢N)−1⁢P=P⁢(1−N⁢P)−1,J=I+N⁢c,Z=c+M⁢J.M=(1-PN)^{-1}P=P(1-NP)^{-1},\qquad J=I+Nc,\qquad Z=c+MJ. (3.34)

All products use ordinary transposes, not complex-conjugate transposes.

Formal construction 3.2 (All-sector point observables).

The formal upper-lateral completion is

D+\displaystyle D^{+} =D0+1π⁢XT⁢Z,\displaystyle=D_{0}+\frac{1}{\pi}X^{T}Z, (3.35)
R+\displaystyle R^{+} =R0+1π⁢[IT⁢c+12⁢cT⁢N⁢c+12⁢JT⁢M⁢J],\displaystyle=R_{0}+\frac{1}{\pi}\left[I^{T}c+\frac{1}{2}c^{T}Nc+\frac{1}{2}J^% {T}MJ\right], (3.36)
E+\displaystyle E^{+} =2⁢π⁢R+−2.\displaystyle=2\pi R^{+}-2. (3.37)

The lower-lateral convention is its conjugate for real positive vv. At a fixed power Λn\Lambda^{n}, indices larger than nn cannot contribute, and the inverse in equation (3.34) is a finite path expansion at that order.

Expanding M=P+P⁢N⁢P+P⁢N⁢P⁢N⁢P+⋯M=P+PNP+PNPNP+\cdots accounts for every internal path. The vector cc accounts for external residues, while N⁢cNc and the matrix products generate mixed paths. In particular,

R1\displaystyle R_{1} =4⁢i⁢C1⁢I1,\displaystyle=4\mathrm{i}C_{1}I_{1}, (3.38)
R2\displaystyle R_{2} =4⁢i⁢C2⁢I2−8⁢π⁢C12⁢N11+S22⁢π⁢I12.\displaystyle=4\mathrm{i}C_{2}I_{2}-8\pi C_{1}^{2}N_{11}+\frac{S_{2}}{2\pi}I_{% 1}^{2}. (3.39)

The direct two-source residue is only one term in the full second sector. Its constant real coefficient is e−2e^{-2}; at the next level the corresponding real constant is 8⁢2/(3⁢e3)8\sqrt{2}/(3e^{3}). Both emerge automatically from the code, without insertion as input.

The external factor 4⁢π⁢i⁢Cr4\pi\mathrm{i}C_{r} depends on the full lateral contour prescription. A half-residue replacement fails the observed ambiguity-cancellation test. The physical finite-interval equation has a unique solution, so no sector amplitude is fitted. Nevertheless, the identification of formal construction 3.2 with that unique solution after complete resummation is a separate analytic statement; it is not proved merely by choosing these constants.

3.6 Algebraic compatibility with the exact identities#

The constant-source boundary amplitude and the endpoint response have the formal representations

χ=a0+XT⁢M⁢a,H=h+aT⁢Z.\chi=a_{0}+X^{T}Ma,\qquad H=h+a^{T}Z. (3.40)

If κr⁢s=2⁢r⁢δr⁢s\kappa_{rs}=2r\delta_{rs}, the ODEs imply

N˙=κ⁢N+N⁢κ+a⁢aT,M˙=−κ⁢M−M⁢κ+M⁢a⁢aT⁢M,Z˙=−κ⁢Z+M⁢a⁢H.\dot{N}=\kappa N+N\kappa+aa^{T},\quad\dot{M}=-\kappa M-M\kappa+Maa^{T}M,\quad% \dot{Z}=-\kappa Z+MaH. (3.41)

Together with X˙=κ⁢X+a0⁢a\dot{X}=\kappa X+a_{0}a, these identities give

D˙=χ⁢Hπ,R˙=H22⁢π.\dot{D}=\frac{\chi H}{\pi},\qquad\dot{R}=\frac{H^{2}}{2\pi}. (3.42)

Hence equation (2.13) is obeyed sector by sector. Conversely, after generating DD and χ\chi, one can obtain RnR_{n} by the independent recursion

(∂b−2⁢n)⁢Rn=π2⁢∑k=0nUk⁢Un−k,D˙χ=∑n≥0Λn⁢Un.(\partial_{b}-2n)R_{n}=\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{k=0}^{n}U_{k}U_{n-k},\qquad\frac{% \dot{D}}{\chi}=\sum_{n\geq 0}\Lambda^{n}U_{n}. (3.43)

The distributed implementation checks the matrix formula, a direct path enumeration, and equation (3.43) against one another. Their agreement is an algebraic check, distinct from comparison with TBA.

4 High-order generation and numerical validation#

4.1 Coefficient generation and independent checks#

The retained production calculation evaluates the commuting flows through order 210 and extracts the scalar seeds through v208v^{208}. The distributed point-observable files retain powers through v200v^{200}, with the integer and half-integer power families stored separately where both occur, at levels 0≤n≤120\leq n\leq 12. Thus there are approximately 200 coefficients per power family, not just a handful of fitted asymptotic terms.

The production implementation substitutes high-precision numerical values of the times before the high-order run, while retaining an auxiliary flow parameter. It avoids expanding separate symbolic zeta monomials at high order. It is not a fully symbolic 210th-order polynomial in the zeta values. The retained C++ flow run took 736.5 seconds and approximately 1.3 GB in its recorded environment; these are provenance data, not a controlled benchmark against another implementation.

There are several distinct validations.

The constant-source check is unusually stringent, but it must not be overinterpreted: it does not provide an independent 208-order Volin computation of the new endpoint function. The endpoint extension instead has exact low-order checks, algebraic compatibility tests, and the independent nonperturbative comparisons below.

4.2 Reference solutions and certified error bounds#

For the reference integral equations we use an even-Chebyshev expansion after rescaling to [−1,1][-1,1]. The Lorentzian kernel acts on the modes by explicit recurrences, turning the equation into a dense linear system. This is the efficient spectral strategy used in Ristivojevic’s weak-coupling calculations [18]; independent Gauss–Legendre Nyström calculations are also retained. The latter approach is standard for Fredholm determinants and their numerical control [19].

To distinguish convergence diagnostics from actual enclosures, we also compute a uniform residual certificate. If fappf_{\rm app} is any explicit approximate profile and

rapp=(I−KQ)⁢fapp−g,r_{\rm app}=(I-K_{Q})f_{\rm app}-g, (4.1)

then equation (1.5) yields

‖fapp−f‖∞≤‖rapp‖∞1−(2/π)⁢arctan⁡Q.\|f_{\rm app}-f\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\|r_{\rm app}\|_{\infty}}{1-(2/\pi)\arctan Q}. (4.2)

Interval-enclosed quadrature nodes and weights, collocation residuals, and a complex-ellipse quadrature bound give the enclosures in table 3. Details appear in appendix F. They are bounds for the reference Fredholm solutions, not for a Padé approximant.

4.3 Lateral Borel–Leroy–Padé summation#

For each power family, factor out the lowest power vμv^{\mu} and retain explicit nonpositive powers and logarithms. For the remaining series A⁢(v)=∑k≥0ak⁢vkA(v)=\sum_{k\geq 0}a_{k}v^{k}, use

ℬℓ⁢A⁢(t)=∑k≥0akΓ⁢(k+ℓ)⁢tk,𝒮+⁢A⁢(v)=∫0∞⁢ei⁢ϕe−t⁢tℓ−1⁢ℬℓ⁢A⁢(v⁢t)⁢dt.\mathcal{B}_{\ell}A(t)=\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{a_{k}}{\Gamma(k+\ell)}t^{k},\qquad% \mathcal{S}_{+}A(v)=\int_{0}^{\infty e^{i\phi}}e^{-t}t^{\ell-1}\mathcal{B}_{% \ell}A(vt)\mathrm{d}t. (4.3)

Near-diagonal Padé approximants replace the truncated Borel transform. For ℓ=3/2\ell=3/2, generalized Gauss–Laguerre quadrature with weight e−x⁢x1/2e^{-x}x^{1/2} is used after rotation t=ei⁢ϕ⁢xt=e^{i\phi}x. The phase ei⁢ℓ⁢ϕe^{i\ell\phi} and the remaining factor e−(ei⁢ϕ−1)⁢xe^{-(e^{i\phi}-1)x} are included explicitly. Ordinary Laguerre quadrature without the endpoint weight creates a false numerical floor. General resurgence conventions follow Ref. [20]; the fixed-source comparisons of Ref. [2] motivate the finite-angle implementation.

Two further choices substantially improve the precision. First, resumming the primitive functions and then assembling equations (3.35) and (3.36) is more stable than separately resumming every expanded sector. Formal multiplicative compatibility does not make finite-order Padé approximants equally accurate. Second, the decaying Green solution of equation (3.30) is

Ir⁢(b)=−12⁢r⁢∫0∞e−y⁢ar⁢(b+y2⁢r)⁢h⁢(b+y2⁢r)⁢dy.I_{r}(b)=-\frac{1}{2r}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-y}a_{r}\!\left(b+\frac{y}{2r}\right% )h\!\left(b+\frac{y}{2r}\right)\mathrm{d}y. (4.4)

It avoids reconstructing by Padé the singularity generated by formal ODE inversion. Replacing the r=1r=1 endpoint block by equation (4.4) is particularly useful.

The primary Q=0.9Q=0.9 comparison uses seed truncation T0=198T_{0}=198, endpoint order TI=190T_{I}=190, fixed-source order TF=130T_{F}=130, 512 quadrature nodes, and ϕ=0.40\phi=0.40. The Green replacement uses order 190, an inner angle 0.50, 384 inner nodes, and 32 outer nodes. Working precision is 200 decimal digits, with the stated lower evaluation precision inside the nested integral recorded in the parameter file. The principal calculation was rerun from the supplied coefficients for this manuscript.

All parameter scans are retained, including failures. Small-angle 256-node quadrature generated an error floor near 10−1310^{-13}–10−1410^{-14} in early tests; increasing coefficient count did not cure it. The tested one-cut conformal transformations were not superior, and some near-diagonal Padé approximants were defective. No defective calculation is used as evidence for a resolved sector, and the plotted stability range is not replaced by the best single approximant.

4.4 Resolved point-observable sectors#

For F=DF=D or RR, define the independent remainder and prediction

ℛn−1F=FTBA−ℜ⁡𝒮+⁢∑k=0n−1Λk⁢Fk,𝒫nF=ℜ⁡𝒮+⁢(Λn⁢Fn).\mathcal{R}_{n-1}^{F}=F_{\rm TBA}-\Re\mathcal{S}_{+}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\Lambda^{k% }F_{k},\qquad\mathcal{P}_{n}^{F}=\Re\mathcal{S}_{+}(\Lambda^{n}F_{n}). (4.5)

No TBA values are used to construct 𝒫nF\mathcal{P}_{n}^{F}. The remainder includes all following sectors, so the ratio need not equal one even with exact resummation.

The approximately 0.3%0.3\%–0.4%0.4\% excess in successive central-density ratios is mainly the next sector, not an error estimate for the current one. In the primary run the real errors after including n=8n=8 are 1.84×10−221.84\times 10^{-22} for DD and 8.62×10−228.62\times 10^{-22} for RR. These favorable values alone do not establish the eighth sector.

The stability ensemble varies T0=194,196,197,198,199,200T_{0}=194,196,197,198,199,200 and ϕ=0.40,0.55\phi=0.40,0.55. The post-eighth-sector error divided by the magnitude of sector seven lies in

D:[−0.00143,0.00117],R:[−0.00785,0.00352].D:\ [-0.00143,0.00117],\qquad R:\ [-0.00785,0.00352]. (4.6)

The same reasonable settings change the eighth-sector remainder/prediction ratio for RR substantially, from about 0.850.85 to 1.881.88. We therefore classify sector seven as resolved at approximately the percent level or better in this ensemble, and sector eight as unresolved.

A separate, weaker-coupling test at Q=2Q=2 gives ℛ4R/𝒫5R=1.00001599\mathcal{R}^{R}_{4}/\mathcal{P}^{R}_{5}=1.00001599 for a fifth-sector contribution of approximately 1.15×10−281.15\times 10^{-28}. At this value of QQ the sixth-sector signal is already below the retained resummation uncertainty. The energy ratios are identical to those of RR, because En=2⁢π⁢RnE_{n}=2\pi R_{n} for n≥1n\geq 1; they are not a third independent validation.

The observation that principal sums agree to many digits should not be conflated with a proof of an infinite resummed trans-series. The certified reference error is negligible at the resolved sector scales; the remaining uncertainty is the analytic-continuation and finite-order Padé error on the trans-series side.

5 The Fredholm determinant and its sector selection rule#

The determinant is simpler than the point observables in one important respect: proposition 2.1 needs only the constant-source boundary value χ\chi, not the new endpoint seed hh. Its formal nonperturbative content is therefore inherited from the fixed-source path construction.

5.1 A complete even-sector recursion#

The boundary amplitude in equation (3.40) contains only even powers of Λ\Lambda, since Pr⁢r∝Λ2⁢rP_{rr}\propto\Lambda^{2r} and no external residue cc occurs. In the bb-coordinate, equation (2.8) has the same form:

𝒢¨=−(∂blog⁡χ)2.\ddot{\mathcal{G}}=-(\partial_{b}\log\chi)^{2}. (5.1)

Expand

p=∂blog⁡χ=∑n≥0Λn⁢pn,𝒢=∑n≥0Λn⁢𝒢n.p=\partial_{b}\log\chi=\sum_{n\geq 0}\Lambda^{n}p_{n},\qquad\mathcal{G}=\sum_{% n\geq 0}\Lambda^{n}\mathcal{G}_{n}. (5.2)

For every n>0n>0,

(∂b−2⁢n)2⁢𝒢n=−∑k=0npk⁢pn−k.(\partial_{b}-2n)^{2}\mathcal{G}_{n}=-\sum_{k=0}^{n}p_{k}p_{n-k}. (5.3)

Applying equation (3.31) twice determines the sector; growing homogeneous terms are excluded. It follows that

𝒢2⁢r+1=0.\mathcal{G}_{2r+1}=0. (5.4)

Thus the first allowed formal determinant sector is Λ2=e−4⁢π⁢Q\Lambda^{2}=e^{-4\pi Q}, even though the elementary external-source scale for the lattice point observables is Λ=e−2⁢π⁢Q\Lambda=e^{-2\pi Q}. This refines, rather than contradicts, an ansatz that allows arbitrary multiples of the candidate scale: its odd determinant coefficients vanish in this convention.

Exact symbolic arithmetic gives

𝒢2\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{2} =−ie2⁢(v2+5⁢v28+61⁢v364+⋯),\displaystyle=-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{e^{2}}\left(\frac{v}{2}+\frac{5v^{2}}{8}+% \frac{61v^{3}}{64}+\cdots\right), (5.5)
𝒢4\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{4} =1e4⁢[14+(18−i)⁢v+(732−13⁢i8)⁢v2+⋯],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{e^{4}}\left[\frac{1}{4}+\left(\frac{1}{8}-\mathrm{i}% \right)v+\left(\frac{7}{32}-\frac{13\mathrm{i}}{8}\right)v^{2}+\cdots\right], (5.6)
𝒢6\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{6} =1e6⁢[169+(23−13⁢i4)⁢v+(98−91⁢i16)⁢v2+⋯].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{e^{6}}\left[\frac{16}{9}+\left(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{13% \mathrm{i}}{4}\right)v+\left(\frac{9}{8}-\frac{91\mathrm{i}}{16}\right)v^{2}+% \cdots\right]. (5.7)

The purely imaginary formal coefficients in equation (5.5) do not permit that sector to be omitted. The real part of a lateral sum is not the lateral sum of coefficientwise real parts. Exponentiating 𝒢\mathcal{G} gives the corresponding determinant sectors.

5.2 Perturbative normalization and the Fisher–Hartwig constant#

The symbol is σ⁢(p)=1−e−|p|\sigma(p)=1-e^{-|p|}. Its root at zero produces the logarithmic term in the Wiener–Hopf/Fisher–Hartwig asymptotics [21, 22]. In the interval-length convention 2⁢Q2Q, write

𝒢0⁢(Q)=−π⁢Q3+14⁢log⁡Q+βFH+⋯.\mathcal{G}_{0}(Q)=-\frac{\pi Q}{3}+\frac{1}{4}\log Q+\beta_{\rm FH}+\cdots. (5.8)

The curvature equation does not fix the asymptotic slope and constant by local large-QQ integration. The extensive term follows from the symbol integral; the constant requires the Fisher–Hartwig normalization or the exact finite-interval formula equation (2.9).

Evaluating the single-root normalization gives

βFH=−16+712log2+34logπ+6ζ′(−1).\boxed{\displaystyle\beta_{\rm FH}=-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{7}{12}\log 2+\frac{3}{4}% \log\pi+6\zeta^{\prime}(-1).} (5.9)

Numerically,

βFH=0.10368974084431265248410462290871317519529457⁢….\beta_{\rm FH}=0.10368974084431265248410462290871317519529457\ldots. (5.10)

The calculation uses the Fourier transform

g⁢(t)=12⁢π⁢t2−coth⁡(π⁢t)2⁢tg(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi t^{2}}-\frac{\coth(\pi t)}{2t} (5.11)

and the regularized integral

CE=limL→∞[∫0Lt⁢g⁢(t)2⁢dt−14⁢log⁡L]=γE4−16+14⁢log⁡(2⁢π)+3⁢ζ′⁢(−1).C_{E}=\lim_{L\to\infty}\left[\int_{0}^{L}tg(t)^{2}\mathrm{d}t-\frac{1}{4}\log L% \right]=\frac{\gamma_{E}}{4}-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{4}\log(2\pi)+3\zeta^{\prime}% (-1). (5.12)

The Barnes-GG factor and the length conversion yield equation (5.9); details are in appendix C. This is an analytic evaluation under the standard single-root normalization, not a fit. A self-contained verification of every limiting smooth-factor hypothesis of the general Fisher–Hartwig theorem is not supplied here. The independent determinant comparison is an especially sensitive check of the normalization.

The perturbative expansion is

𝒢0=\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{0}={} −b3−14⁢log⁡v+βFH−14⁢log⁡(2⁢π)−18⁢v−1148⁢v2+27⁢ζ⁢(3)−109288⁢v3+⋯.\displaystyle-\frac{b}{3}-\frac{1}{4}\log v+\beta_{\rm FH}-\frac{1}{4}\log(2% \pi)-\frac{1}{8}v-\frac{11}{48}v^{2}+\frac{27\zeta(3)-109}{288}v^{3}+\cdots. (5.13)

In terms of LQ=log⁡(16⁢π⁢Q)L_{Q}=\log(16\pi Q),

𝒢0=−π⁢Q3+14⁢log⁡Q+βFH+2⁢LQ+116⁢π⁢Q+−6⁢LQ2+6⁢LQ+1192⁢π2⁢Q2+⋯.\mathcal{G}_{0}=-\frac{\pi Q}{3}+\frac{1}{4}\log Q+\beta_{\rm FH}+\frac{2L_{Q}% +1}{16\pi Q}+\frac{-6L_{Q}^{2}+6L_{Q}+1}{192\pi^{2}Q^{2}}+\cdots. (5.14)

The September source gives the leading determinant form with an unspecified constant. Equations (5.9) and (5.3) are the normalization and sector refinements needed to make the comparison quantitative.

5.3 Independent determinant comparison#

We retain 180 perturbative orders per determinant sector through Λ8\Lambda^{8}. The exact comparison uses parity-resolved arbitrary-precision Nyström determinants, not integration of the trans-series for χ\chi. At Q=0.9Q=0.9,

𝒢num=−0.7086944201743600894700642180647777717417⁢….\mathcal{G}_{\rm num}=-0.7086944201743600894700642180647777717417\ldots. (5.15)

Quadrature sizes 65 and 80 agree to the 65-digit output precision, and the ratio F−/F+F_{-}/F_{+} agrees independently with the boundary value. The principal Borel calculation uses 154 terms, angle 0.450.45, 512 nodes, and 170-digit arithmetic; it was rerun in preparing this manuscript.

After including Λ8\Lambda^{8}, the primary real error is 1.97×10−261.97\times 10^{-26} and the cumulative imaginary part is −4.04×10−26-4.04\times 10^{-26}. The additional settings (150,0.55)(150,0.55) and (158,0.40)(158,0.40), with the same 512 nodes, put the last remainder/prediction ratio in [1.0001683,1.0003237][1.0001683,1.0003237]. This resolves the eighth determinant sector at a few parts in 10410^{4} in the tested ensemble. It does not resolve the eighth sectors of DD or RR, which are numerically different problems.

The coefficient of Λ2\Lambda^{2} has a real lateral contribution comparable to the subsequent Λ4\Lambda^{4} contribution. Accordingly, its remainder/prediction ratio alone is close to one half rather than one. This is another reason to retain complex lateral sectors and test the complete sequence of cancellations. The complete table, including the perturbative and second sectors, is supplied rather than hidden.

6 A uniform spectral-determinant limit and spectral refinements#

Let 1>μ0⁢(Q)≥μ1⁢(Q)≥⋯>01>\mu_{0}(Q)\geq\mu_{1}(Q)\geq\cdots>0 be the eigenvalues of KQK_{Q}. They are operator eigenvalues, not physical excitation energies. Upon scaling x=Q⁢yx=Qy and setting h=1/Qh=1/Q, the operator becomes

Th=P(−1,1)⁢e−h⁢|∂|⁢P(−1,1).T_{h}=P_{(-1,1)}e^{-h|\partial|}P_{(-1,1)}. (6.1)

This is a compression of the full-line Cauchy semigroup. At nonzero hh it is not the continuously killed interval semigroup. The limiting generator is the restricted half-Laplacian AA: functions are extended by zero outside (−1,1)(-1,1) before the Fourier multiplier |p||p| is applied. The spectral square root of the ordinary Dirichlet Laplacian is a different operator.

Sant’Ana’s September revision already identifies the fixed-mode limit

Q⁢[1−μj−1⁢(Q)]⟶λj,Q[1-\mu_{j-1}(Q)]\longrightarrow\lambda_{j}, (6.2)

where λj\lambda_{j} are the eigenvalues of AA. The fractional-operator spectral input is established in Ref. [23]. The new objective is a simultaneous analytic object containing all these limits, suitable for a later uniform eigenvalue trans-series.

6.1 Regularized deformed determinant#

Define

F⁢(z,Q)=det(I−z⁢KQ),BQ=1Q⁢KQ⁢(I−KQ)−1.F(z,Q)=\det(I-zK_{Q}),\qquad B_{Q}=\frac{1}{Q}K_{Q}(I-K_{Q})^{-1}. (6.3)

Factoring the two operators gives the exact identity

𝔇Q(u):=F⁢(1+u/Q,Q)F⁢(1,Q)eu⁢Tr⁡BQ=det(I−uBQ)2,\mathfrak{D}_{Q}(u):=\frac{F(1+u/Q,Q)}{F(1,Q)}e^{u\operatorname{Tr}B_{Q}}=\det% {}_{2}(I-uB_{Q}), (6.4)

where

det(I−uB)2=∏j≥1(1−uβj)eu⁢βj.\det{}_{2}(I-uB)=\prod_{j\geq 1}(1-u\beta_{j})e^{u\beta_{j}}. (6.5)

The exponential subtraction cannot be omitted: the limiting inverse is Hilbert–Schmidt but not trace class.

Theorem 6.1 (Uniform spectral-determinant limit).

As Q→∞Q\to\infty,

𝔇Q(u)⟶det(I−uA−1)2\mathfrak{D}_{Q}(u)\longrightarrow\det{}_{2}(I-uA^{-1}) (6.6)

locally uniformly for complex uu. In particular, its fixed low zeros

uj⁢(Q)=Q⁢[μj−1⁢(Q)−1−1]u_{j}(Q)=Q[\mu_{j-1}(Q)^{-1}-1] (6.7)

converge to the corresponding eigenvalues λj\lambda_{j}.

Proof.

For zero-extended ff, the quadratic forms

qh⁢(f)=12⁢π⁢∫ℝ1−e−h⁢|p|h⁢|f^⁢(p)|2⁢dpq_{h}(f)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1-e^{-h|p|}}{h}|\widehat{f}(p)|^% {2}\mathrm{d}p (6.8)

increase to the form of AA as h↓0h\downarrow 0. The min–max upper bound follows by testing on fixed eigenfunctions of AA. Bounded qhq_{h} controls the Fourier tail: for fixed MM and sufficiently small hh, its mass above MM is at most 2⁢C/M2C/M. Together with the fixed spatial support, this yields compactness of bounded-energy eigenvectors. The lower variational bound then proves equation (6.2). Consequently,

βj⁢(Q)=μj−1⁢(Q)Q⁢[1−μj−1⁢(Q)]⟶λj−1.\beta_{j}(Q)=\frac{\mu_{j-1}(Q)}{Q[1-\mu_{j-1}(Q)]}\longrightarrow\lambda_{j}^% {-1}. (6.9)

It remains to control the product uniformly in jj. Positivity of the Cauchy kernel permits dropping the restrictions on intermediate integration points in a trace cycle, giving

Tr⁡Thm≤2π⁢m⁢h,m=1,2,….\operatorname{Tr}T_{h}^{m}\leq\frac{2}{\pi mh},\qquad m=1,2,\ldots. (6.10)

Since j⁢μj−1m≤Tr⁡Thmj\mu_{j-1}^{m}\leq\operatorname{Tr}T_{h}^{m}, choosing m=⌈1/(−log⁡μj−1)⌉m=\lceil 1/(-\log\mu_{j-1})\rceil when −log⁡μj−1≤1-\log\mu_{j-1}\leq 1, and m=1m=1 otherwise, yields

0≤βj⁢(Q)≤2⁢e2π⁢j.0\leq\beta_{j}(Q)\leq\frac{2e^{2}}{\pi j}. (6.11)

The squared majorant is summable. The tails of the regularized products therefore converge uniformly on compact uu-sets, while every finite head converges termwise. This proves equation (6.6). Zero convergence follows either from the explicit uju_{j} formula or from local uniform convergence with multiplicities. ∎

The theorem is a scaling result, not a finite-QQ trans-series for individual eigenvalues. It identifies the correct spectral window z=1+u/Qz=1+u/Q. A trans-series evaluated only at z=1z=1 cannot determine the displaced zeros in that window.

6.2 An exact inverse-square spectral sum#

The published Green kernel of the restricted half-Laplacian is [23]

GA⁢(x,y)=1π⁢log⁡1−x⁢y+1−x2⁢1−y2|x−y|.G_{A}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\pi}\log\frac{1-xy+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\sqrt{1-y^{2}}}{|x-y|}. (6.12)

Squaring and integrating gives an explicit trace.

Proposition 6.2.
Tr⁡A−2=∑j≥1λj−2=2+7⁢ζ⁢(3)π2=1.055199164919687124734801779611789⁢….\operatorname{Tr}A^{-2}=\sum_{j\geq 1}\lambda_{j}^{-2}=\frac{2+7\zeta(3)}{\pi^% {2}}=1.055199164919687124734801779611789\ldots. (6.13)
Proof.

Set x=tanh⁡tx=\tanh t, y=tanh⁡sy=\tanh s. The logarithm in equation (6.12) becomes log⁡coth⁡(|t−s|/2)\log\coth(|t-s|/2). The convolution identity

∫ℝsech2⁡t⁢sech2⁡(t−u)⁢d⁢t=4⁢(u⁢coth⁡u−1)⁢csch2⁡u\int_{\mathbb{R}}\operatorname{sech}^{2}t\operatorname{sech}^{2}(t-u)\mathrm{d% }t=4(u\coth u-1)\operatorname{csch}^{2}u (6.14)

reduces the trace to a single integral. With z=tanh⁡(u/2)z=\tanh(u/2) this is

Tr⁡A−2=4π2⁢∫01[(z−3−z)⁢atanh⁡z−z−2+1]⁢log2⁡z⁢d⁢z.\operatorname{Tr}A^{-2}=\frac{4}{\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{1}[(z^{-3}-z)\operatorname{% atanh}z-z^{-2}+1]\log^{2}z\mathrm{d}z. (6.15)

Expand atanh⁡z\operatorname{atanh}z after the displayed cancellation of the singular term. Integrating each monomial and summing the resulting partial fractions gives 1/2+7⁢ζ⁢(3)/41/2+7\zeta(3)/4 for the integral. The explicit summation is given in appendix D. ∎

An independent quadrature agrees to approximately 63 decimal digits. We use the sum as an analytic normalization and numerical check; no claim of first publication of this identity is needed. It fixes

logdet(I−uA−1)2=−2+7⁢ζ⁢(3)2⁢π2u2+O(u3).\log\det{}_{2}(I-uA^{-1})=-\frac{2+7\zeta(3)}{2\pi^{2}}u^{2}+O(u^{3}). (6.16)

For efficient spectral computation, an energy-orthonormal basis is

en⁢(x)=2π⁢n⁢sin⁡(n⁢arccos⁡x),n≥1.e_{n}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi n}}\sin(n\arccos x),\qquad n\geq 1. (6.17)

The compact embedding matrix, isospectral to A−1A^{-1}, has entries

Cm⁢n=2π⁢m⁢n⁢[11−(m−n)2−11−(m+n)2]C_{mn}=\frac{2}{\pi\sqrt{mn}}\left[\frac{1}{1-(m-n)^{2}}-\frac{1}{1-(m+n)^{2}}\right] (6.18)

for equal parities and zero for opposite parities. This follows from A⁢[1−x2⁢Un−1⁢(x)]=n⁢Un−1⁢(x)A[\sqrt{1-x^{2}}U_{n-1}(x)]=nU_{n-1}(x) and direct trigonometric integration. It avoids singular-kernel quadrature for the limiting operator.

6.3 The leading gap and its logarithmic refinement#

For completeness, the elementary bounds

1−2π⁢arctan⁡Q≤1−μ0⁢(Q)≤3⁢π8⁢Q1-\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan Q\leq 1-\mu_{0}(Q)\leq\frac{3\pi}{8Q} (6.19)

follow from the maximal row sum and the trial function 1−y2\sqrt{1-y^{2}}, respectively. Together with equation (6.2), they confirm the 1/Q1/Q scale already identified in the September revision. The first fractional eigenvalue is approximately 1.157773883697591.15777388369759; the unnormalized operator gap of Ref. [1] is 2⁢π⁢(1−μ0)2\pi(1-\mu_{0}).

There is a further logarithm at the next algebraic order. For an L2L^{2}-normalized AA-eigenfunction, let

ϕj⁢(x)∼c±⁢dist⁡(x,∂(−1,1))\phi_{j}(x)\sim c_{\pm}\sqrt{\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial(-1,1))} (6.20)

at the two endpoints. The fractional Pohozaev identity [24] gives

c+2+c−2=4⁢λjπ.c_{+}^{2}+c_{-}^{2}=\frac{4\lambda_{j}}{\pi}. (6.21)

Its nonoscillatory Fourier tail is π⁢(c+2+c−2)/(4⁢|p|3)\pi(c_{+}^{2}+c_{-}^{2})/(4|p|^{3}). Inserting this into equation (6.8) gives, for the fixed limiting eigenfunction,

qh⁢(ϕj)−q⁢(ϕj)=−λj2⁢π⁢h⁢log⁡(1/h)+O⁢(h).q_{h}(\phi_{j})-q(\phi_{j})=-\frac{\lambda_{j}}{2\pi}h\log(1/h)+O(h). (6.22)

The oscillatory cross-endpoint term does not produce the logarithm.

Conjecture 6.3 (First actual-eigenvalue correction).

For each fixed mode,

1−μj−1⁢(Q)=λjQ−λj2⁢π⁢log⁡QQ2−CjQ2+o⁢(Q−2).1-\mu_{j-1}(Q)=\frac{\lambda_{j}}{Q}-\frac{\lambda_{j}}{2\pi}\frac{\log Q}{Q^{% 2}}-\frac{C_{j}}{Q^{2}}+o(Q^{-2}). (6.23)

The logarithmic coefficient in equation (6.22) is derived, but promotion to equation (6.23) requires a perturbed-eigenfunction estimate that is not supplied. It would be incorrect to identify the Rayleigh calculation with a proof of the actual eigenvalue expansion.

We test the predicted, rather than fitted, logarithmic coefficient for four modes using a Toeplitz/Galerkin eigensolver, two cell resolutions, and Richardson extrapolation. The data extend through Q=4096Q=4096 for four modes and through 81928192 for the first gap. After subtracting the predicted logarithm, the first constant estimate increases from 1.049131.04913 at Q=128Q=128 to 1.069151.06915 at Q=4096Q=4096. The other modes stabilize similarly; the constants themselves are not assigned closed forms.

Individual exponentially small eigenvalue corrections remain uncomputed. Before extracting them, the algebraic and logarithmic background must be controlled uniformly near the zeros of equation (6.4). The determinant trans-series at z=1z=1 alone cannot provide that control.

7 Low-temperature thermodynamics from the same endpoint data#

The finite-temperature TBA and the low-energy gapless interpretation of the negative-spin model are established in Ref. [17]. We use that framework, with the Yang–Yang thermodynamic convention [25], to derive the next temperature coefficient and connect it to the scalar endpoint functions. This section sets κ=1\kappa=1, so the bare energy is

e0⁢(x)=−21+x2.e_{0}(x)=-\frac{2}{1+x^{2}}. (7.1)

The free energy and the dimensionless positive function E=2⁢π⁢R−2E=2\pi R-2 should not be confused: the physical ground-state energy at this coupling is −E-E.

7.1 Dressed energy, sound velocity, and compressibility#

The zero-temperature dressed energy satisfies

(I−KQ)⁢ϵ0=e0−μ,ϵ0⁢(x)=−2⁢π⁢ρQ⁢(x)−μ⁢fQ⁢(x),ϵ0⁢(Q)=0.(I-K_{Q})\epsilon_{0}=e_{0}-\mu,\qquad\epsilon_{0}(x)=-2\pi\rho_{Q}(x)-\mu f_{% Q}(x),\qquad\epsilon_{0}(Q)=0. (7.2)

Therefore

μ=−2⁢π⁢ηχ=−π⁢D′χ2.\mu=-\frac{2\pi\eta}{\chi}=-\frac{\pi D^{\prime}}{\chi^{2}}. (7.3)

Differentiating along the family of ground states gives ∂Qϵ0⁢(x)=−μ′⁢fQ⁢(x)\partial_{Q}\epsilon_{0}(x)=-\mu^{\prime}f_{Q}(x), because the boundary terms are proportional to ϵ0⁢(±Q)=0\epsilon_{0}(\pm Q)=0. With u=ϵ0′⁢(Q)>0u=\epsilon_{0}^{\prime}(Q)>0, where this prime is the rapidity derivative in the definition of uu, one obtains u=μ′⁢χu=\mu^{\prime}\chi. Thus

vs=u2⁢π⁢η=−dd⁢Q⁢log⁡(−μ),KLutt=χ2,𝒦:=∂D∂μ=χ2π⁢vs.v_{s}=\frac{u}{2\pi\eta}=-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}Q}\log(-\mu),\qquad K_{% \rm Lutt}=\chi^{2},\qquad\mathcal{K}:=\frac{\partial D}{\partial\mu}=\frac{% \chi^{2}}{\pi v_{s}}. (7.4)

All formal weak-coupling sectors of these quantities follow by ordinary series differentiation and division. No new endpoint seed is required.

For example,

μ0⁢(v)\displaystyle\mu_{0}(v) =−4⁢π⁢v⁢[1+2⁢v+(92−π26)⁢v2+O⁢(v3)],\displaystyle=-4\pi v\left[1+2v+\left(\frac{9}{2}-\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\right)v^{2% }+O(v^{3})\right], (7.5)
vs,0⁢(v)\displaystyle v_{s,0}(v) =2⁢π⁢v⁢[1+3⁢v+(8−π23)⁢v2+O⁢(v3)].\displaystyle=2\pi v\left[1+3v+\left(8-\frac{\pi^{2}}{3}\right)v^{2}+O(v^{3})% \right]. (7.6)

These formulas describe the Fermi-point dispersion, not the full physical excitation spectrum at arbitrary momentum.

7.2 A quartic Sommerfeld coefficient#

The nonlinear thermal equation and grand potential are

ϵT⁢(x)\displaystyle\epsilon_{T}(x) =e0⁢(x)−μ−T⁢∫ℝK⁢(x−y)⁢log⁡(1+e−ϵT⁢(y)/T)⁢dy,\displaystyle=e_{0}(x)-\mu-T\int_{\mathbb{R}}K(x-y)\log(1+e^{-\epsilon_{T}(y)/% T})\mathrm{d}y, (7.7)
Ω⁢(T,μ)\displaystyle\Omega(T,\mu) =−T⁢∫ℝK⁢(x)⁢log⁡(1+e−ϵT⁢(x)/T)⁢dx.\displaystyle=-T\int_{\mathbb{R}}K(x)\log(1+e^{-\epsilon_{T}(x)/T})\mathrm{d}x. (7.8)

Write

Ω⁢(T,μ)=Ω0⁢(μ)+ω2⁢(μ)⁢T2+ω4⁢(μ)⁢T4+O⁢(T6),ω2=−π6⁢vs.\Omega(T,\mu)=\Omega_{0}(\mu)+\omega_{2}(\mu)T^{2}+\omega_{4}(\mu)T^{4}+O(T^{6% }),\qquad\omega_{2}=-\frac{\pi}{6v_{s}}. (7.9)

The quadratic coefficient is the standard one-component gapless result. Its complete formal weak-coupling series is inherited from equation (7.4).

For the next term, put c1=π2/6c_{1}=\pi^{2}/6, c2=7⁢π4/360c_{2}=7\pi^{4}/360, and ϵT=ϵ0+T2⁢ϵ2+⋯\epsilon_{T}=\epsilon_{0}+T^{2}\epsilon_{2}+\cdots. Sommerfeld expansion at the two Fermi points yields

(I−KQ)⁢ϵ2⁢(x)=−c1u⁢[K⁢(x−Q)+K⁢(x+Q)],(I-K_{Q})\epsilon_{2}(x)=-\frac{c_{1}}{u}[K(x-Q)+K(x+Q)], (7.10)

so

ϵ2⁢(x)=−c1u⁢[ℛQ⁢(x,Q)+ℛQ⁢(x,−Q)].\epsilon_{2}(x)=-\frac{c_{1}}{u}[\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,Q)+\mathscr{R}_{Q}(x,-Q)]. (7.11)

Use the local energy coordinate z=ϵ0⁢(x)z=\epsilon_{0}(x) near x=Qx=Q, with ∂z=(∂xϵ0)−1⁢∂x\partial_{z}=(\partial_{x}\epsilon_{0})^{-1}\partial_{x}. The result is

ω4=−2[ρ⁢ϵ222⁢∂xϵ0−c1∂z(ρ⁢ϵ2∂xϵ0)+c2∂z2(ρ∂xϵ0)]x=Q.\boxed{\displaystyle\omega_{4}=-2\left[\frac{\rho\epsilon_{2}^{2}}{2\partial_{% x}\epsilon_{0}}-c_{1}\partial_{z}\!\left(\frac{\rho\epsilon_{2}}{\partial_{x}% \epsilon_{0}}\right)+c_{2}\partial_{z}^{2}\!\left(\frac{\rho}{\partial_{x}% \epsilon_{0}}\right)\right]_{x=Q}.} (7.12)

The density and dressed energy in this expression are continued smoothly through the endpoint by their integral equations. Self-adjointness cancels the otherwise unknown fourth-order dressed-energy correction. The derivation and the reduction of all endpoint derivatives to D,χ,𝒢D,\chi,\mathcal{G} are given in appendix E. Thus equation (7.12) is both a numerical endpoint formula and a coefficient-generating rule for its formal weak-coupling trans-series.

At Q=0.9Q=0.9, the independent ground-state calculation gives

μ=−1.2999150573992906,vs=0.6138856180302584,ω4=−0.6292090698625181.\mu=-1.2999150573992906,\qquad v_{s}=0.6138856180302584,\qquad\omega_{4}=-0.62% 92090698625181. (7.13)

Solving equation (7.7) independently, define

C4⁢(T)=Ω⁢(T,μ)−Ω0⁢(μ)+π⁢T2/(6⁢vs)T4.C_{4}(T)=\frac{\Omega(T,\mu)-\Omega_{0}(\mu)+\pi T^{2}/(6v_{s})}{T^{4}}. (7.14)

Table 8 shows convergence to the endpoint prediction. The tests use ordinary floating-point thermal solves with resolution checks; unlike table 3, they are not interval certificates.

7.3 Fixed-density conversion#

Because D=−∂μΩD=-\partial_{\mu}\Omega, a fixed-density expansion requires

μ⁢(T)=μ0+∂μω2𝒦⁢T2+O⁢(T4).\mu(T)=\mu_{0}+\frac{\partial_{\mu}\omega_{2}}{\mathcal{K}}T^{2}+O(T^{4}). (7.15)

Performing the Legendre transform gives

F⁢(T,D)=F0⁢(D)+ω2⁢T2+[ω4+(∂μω2)22⁢𝒦]⁢T4+O⁢(T6).F(T,D)=F_{0}(D)+\omega_{2}T^{2}+\left[\omega_{4}+\frac{(\partial_{\mu}\omega_{% 2})^{2}}{2\mathcal{K}}\right]T^{4}+O(T^{6}). (7.16)

At the point in equation (7.13), the canonical quartic coefficient is −0.5989616140053465-0.5989616140053465, and the quadratic chemical-potential shift is −0.2153506235547108⁢T2-0.2153506235547108\,T^{2}. The thermal density residuals are near machine precision. In both ensembles the discrepancy of the quartic estimator decreases approximately as T2T^{2}, as expected from the next T6T^{6} term in the free energy.

7.4 High-density behavior and a nontrivial cancellation#

Expanding equation (7.12) in the running coupling gives

ω4⁢(v)=−12880⁢v3+O⁢(v−2),ω4⁢(Q)∼−π3360⁢Q3.\omega_{4}(v)=-\frac{1}{2880v^{3}}+O(v^{-2}),\qquad\omega_{4}(Q)\sim-\frac{\pi% ^{3}}{360}Q^{3}. (7.17)

The potentially larger v−4v^{-4} terms cancel. The three terms in equation (7.12), including the overall factor, contribute respectively

v−4v−31−1/829441/921621/82944−7/2764830−7/34560\begin{array}[]{c|rr}&v^{-4}&v^{-3}\\ \hline\cr 1&-1/82944&1/9216\\ 2&1/82944&-7/27648\\ 3&0&-7/34560\end{array} (7.18)

and sum to equation (7.17). This cancellation is checked symbolically, rather than inferred by fitting a few large-QQ data points.

The weak-coupling sectors of ω2\omega_{2} and ω4\omega_{4} are formally accessible, but the thermal tests here verify their full finite-QQ values, not individually exponentially small thermal sectors. Moreover, a low-temperature expansion at fixed QQ is not automatically uniform when QQ tends to infinity and the sound velocity vanishes.

8 Discussion and well-posed remaining problems#

The continuation goes beyond a candidate exponential scale in three different ways. First, it provides an explicit formal endpoint construction and an all-sector matrix formula, with high-order coefficient generation and independently resolved subleading sectors. Second, exact interval-variation identities determine the determinant and the full lattice profiles from the boundary function. Third, the deformed determinant has a controlled fractional-spectral scaling limit that is stronger than a single leading eigenvalue asymptotic.

These results do not all have the same logical status. The boundary reconstruction and regularized determinant limit are finite-interval or scaling theorems with proofs given above. The endpoint spectral multiplier is a formal construction, not a proved global Borel reconstruction. The first logarithmic actual-eigenvalue correction is a prediction supported by a derived Rayleigh logarithm and four-mode data. The trans-series comparisons are extensive numerical evidence, with a certified reference but an empirically assessed resummation error. These distinctions are part of the result rather than qualifications to be removed by extrapolation.

8.1 One boundary function and the propagation of Stokes data#

The exact Goursat representation changes the main analytic question. The point observables have no independent exact functional freedom once χ\chi is known. Can equation (2.15) be used to derive the endpoint multiplier equation (3.14), the initial response equation (3.16), and the external residues equation (3.33) directly from the fixed-source boundary trans-series?

A proof would need uniform continuation and growth bounds that permit asymptotic and Borel operations under the characteristic double integral. The estimate equation (2.19) proves convergence on finite rectangles but does not justify extending a large-QQ expansion to the origin. This is the principal missing step between the proposed endpoint construction and a global reconstruction theorem. It would also explain structurally why the boundary determinant contains only even powers of Λ\Lambda, while the central observables admit odd ones.

8.2 Uniform spectral resurgence near a zero#

The correct spectral object is now fixed:

𝔇Q(u)=det(I−uA−1)2+finite-Q corrections.\mathfrak{D}_{Q}(u)=\det{}_{2}(I-uA^{-1})+\text{finite-$Q$ corrections}. (8.1)

The meaningful next problem is to compute its algebraic, logarithmic, and exponential deformations uniformly near u=λju=\lambda_{j}, then solve for the moving zeros. Evaluating F⁢(z,Q)F(z,Q) only at z=1z=1 loses precisely the information needed for this step. The exact sum equation (6.13) is a stringent normalization condition for any proposed two-variable construction.

Before resolving an exponentially small eigenvalue sector, one must control the perturbed endpoint eigenfunctions well enough to prove or revise conjecture 6.3. The data do not justify assigning a physical mass gap to these operator eigenvalues. Nor does a Borel singularity identify an attractive Hamiltonian or its Bethe vacuum. An attractive-dual interpretation would require those model choices explicitly; none is supplied here.

8.3 High density and low temperature#

The cancellation in equation (7.17) shows that naive endpoint power counting overestimates the high-density quartic coefficient. It is natural to seek a uniform solution of the nonlinear thermal TBA in a simultaneous low-TT, high-QQ limit, retaining the distinction between fixed density and fixed chemical potential. Two Sommerfeld coefficients do not determine its scaling function or even suffice to prove a common domain of uniformity. This is a genuinely thermodynamic question, not merely a request for more terms of the zero-temperature series.

8.4 A probabilistic meaning of the nonperturbative sectors#

The killed-Cauchy-walk interpretation is already central to Ref. [1] and has classical antecedents in the capacitor problem [26, 27]. Let τ\tau be the first exit step from the interval. For zz within the resolvent domain, the first-step recurrence gives

𝔼x⁢[zτ]=1−(1−z)⁢(I−z⁢KQ)−1⁢1⁢(x).\mathbb{E}_{x}[z^{\tau}]=1-(1-z)(I-zK_{Q})^{-1}1(x). (8.2)

Its derivative at z=1z=1 gives the mean exit time, fQ⁢(x)f_{Q}(x); in particular, D+1D+1 is the central mean exit time. The zeros of F⁢(z,Q)F(z,Q) control singularities of the generating resolvent, subject to possible cancellations for a particular source or evaluation.

This supplies a well-defined alternative to an unspecified physical duality: can the finite-step corrections to the Cauchy-process limit, including exponentially small terms, be associated with identifiable overshoot or repeated-boundary processes? Such an interpretation would connect the density, the spectral determinant, and the origin of distinct observable-dependent sector rules.

8.5 Conclusion#

For the three principal lattice observables, the remaining computational obstruction is no longer an unspecified endpoint function. There is a finite formal algorithm, high-order data, and nontrivial numerical validation. The determinant is even more economical because it needs only the constant-source boundary function. At the exact level, one boundary function reconstructs the full problem; at the spectral level, one regularized determinant controls all fixed low modes.

The strongest unresolved task is analytic rather than numerical: proving that the endpoint formal construction is the Borel representation of the exact boundary-to-bulk solution. Resolving another tiny sector would improve evidence, but would not by itself supply that proof.

Data and reproducibility.#

The companion archive contains the LaTeX manuscript, vector figures, plotting code, all displayed data, three computational modules with their retained coefficient files and parameter scans, and fresh audit logs. Representative endpoint and determinant resummations, interval reference calculations, and all three fast test suites were rerun for this manuscript. The expensive 210-order flow-generation record is retained rather than silently described as a new benchmark. Appendix G gives the exact organization and commands.

Attribution of supplied material.#

The O(3) commuting-flow representation is taken from the unpublished note by Dániel Nógrádi [14]. The endpoint extension and the present synthesis are distinguished from that input. The unpublished note itself is not included in the public supplementary archive.

Appendix A The formal endpoint spectral calculation#

This appendix makes the formal step behind equation (3.16) explicit. At zero odd-zeta times a generalized Jost solution compatible with equation (3.9) is

ak∗=t(1+t2)kek⁢e−2⁢u/2F02(1+k2,1+k2;;wk),t=tanhu=1−2⁢w.a_{k}^{*}=\sqrt{t}\left(\frac{1+t}{2}\right)^{k}e^{ke^{-2u}/2}{}_{2}F_{0}\!% \left(\frac{1+k}{2},\frac{1+k}{2};;\frac{w}{k}\right),\qquad t=\tanh u=\sqrt{1% -2w}. (A.1)

Here F02{}_{2}F_{0} is a formal asymptotic series. Direct substitution verifies (ak∗)′′+2⁢k⁢(ak∗)′=U∗⁢ak∗(a_{k}^{*})^{\prime\prime}+2k(a_{k}^{*})^{\prime}=U_{*}a_{k}^{*} coefficient by coefficient. The zero-source amplitude is treated separately; naive substitution of k=0k=0 is not a uniform limiting procedure.

Writing the hypergeometric factor through Tricomi’s UU converts the source inversion into a spectral contour. On its central cut the phase is

Φ⁢(y)=y+1/2w+12⁢log⁡|y1+y|.\Phi(y)=\frac{y+1/2}{w}+\frac{1}{2}\log\left|\frac{y}{1+y}\right|. (A.2)

Its perturbative root is y=−1/2y=-1/2, with Φ′⁢(−1/2)=(1−2⁢w)/w\Phi^{\prime}(-1/2)=(1-2w)/w. The central Jacobian and amplitude give hcl=2⁢w/t3/2h_{\rm cl}=2\sqrt{w}/t^{3/2}. The other roots approach the cut ends exponentially and are not included in the power-series seed. Dressing the central contribution with the even spectral multiplier gives h∗=ℰ⁢(L∗)⁢hclh_{*}=\mathcal{E}(L_{*})h_{\rm cl}.

The two multiplier calculations used here are elementary:

m⁢(k)⁢m⁢(−k)\displaystyle m(k)m(-k) =π⁢Γ⁢(1+k/2)⁢Γ⁢(1−k/2)Γ⁢((1+k)/2)⁢Γ⁢((1−k)/2)=π⁢k2⁢cot⁡π⁢k2,\displaystyle=\pi\frac{\Gamma(1+k/2)\Gamma(1-k/2)}{\Gamma((1+k)/2)\Gamma((1-k)% /2)}=\frac{\pi k}{2}\cot\frac{\pi k}{2}, (A.3)
[log⁡m⁢(k)]odd\displaystyle[\log m(k)]_{\rm odd} =∑j≥14j−1(2⁢j+1)⁢4j⁢ζ⁢(2⁢j+1)⁢k2⁢j+1=−∑j≥14j⁢τ2⁢j+1⁢k2⁢j+1.\displaystyle=\sum_{j\geq 1}\frac{4^{j}-1}{(2j+1)4^{j}}\zeta(2j+1)k^{2j+1}=-% \sum_{j\geq 1}4^{j}\tau_{2j+1}k^{2j+1}. (A.4)

The first odd term is ζ⁢(3)⁢k3/4\zeta(3)k^{3}/4, a useful sign check. The odd part agrees with the spectral phase of the ordered commuting-flow operators.

This calculation identifies a formal central contribution. It does not provide a uniformly controlled contour deformation separating that contribution from every endpoint term, or the Borel growth estimates needed as the source label tends to zero. The exact reconstruction in theorem 2.2 offers a route to such a proof. Neither algebraic consistency nor high-precision agreement is presented as a substitute for it.

Appendix B Coefficient algorithm and sector arithmetic#

A calculation has two cutoffs: a perturbative order NN and an exponential level nmaxn_{\max}. The finite algorithm is as follows.

  1. 1.

    Generate U∗,a0,∗,h∗U_{*},a_{0,*},h_{*} and w⁢(v)w(v) to guarded order. Retain the flow structure rather than expanding all independent odd-zeta monomials.

  2. 2.

    Integrate the commuting flows to equation (3.11); extract A00,D0,R0A_{00},D_{0},R_{0} with equation (3.20). Fix the known leading constants and check the gauge against the independent ne,nrn_{e},n_{r} input.

  3. 3.

    Generate ar,Xr,Ira_{r},X_{r},I_{r} and the symmetric Nr⁢sN_{rs} needed by the exponential budget, using equations (3.27), (3.28), (3.29) and (3.30).

  4. 4.

    Expand M=P+P⁢N⁢P+⋯M=P+PNP+\cdots only through Λnmax\Lambda^{n_{\max}}. Assemble equations (3.35) and (3.36), and independently recover RR with equation (3.43).

  5. 5.

    For the determinant apply equation (5.3); for thermodynamics apply the scalar endpoint identities, converting QQ- and bb-derivatives consistently.

Scalar series use half-integer Laurent exponents. A dictionary key kk means vk/2v^{k/2}, with complex coefficients stored as pairs of decimal strings. The explicit R0R_{0} logarithm is stored separately. Negative powers are not passed into a Borel transform. Tiny guarded-order numerical remnants are not interpreted as additional leading physical terms.

The first-order inversion equation (3.31) costs linear time in NN after the right-hand side is formed. Products and second-order amplitude recursions incur convolution cost. At fixed nmaxn_{\max} only finitely many labels and paths occur. We do not claim an asymptotically optimal implementation of the scalar flow stage.

For an independent algebraic audit put κ=diag⁡(2,4,6,…)\kappa=\operatorname{diag}(2,4,6,\ldots). Then

P˙=−κ⁢P−P⁢κ,c˙=−κ⁢c,I˙=κ⁢I+a⁢h,X˙=κ⁢X+a0⁢a.\dot{P}=-\kappa P-P\kappa,\quad\dot{c}=-\kappa c,\quad\dot{I}=\kappa I+ah,% \quad\dot{X}=\kappa X+a_{0}a. (B.1)

Differentiating M−1=P−1−NM^{-1}=P^{-1}-N gives

M˙=−κ⁢M−M⁢κ+M⁢a⁢aT⁢M.\dot{M}=-\kappa M-M\kappa+Maa^{T}M. (B.2)

Consequently,

J˙=κ⁢J+a⁢(h+aT⁢c),Z˙=−κ⁢Z+M⁢a⁢(h+aT⁢Z).\dot{J}=\kappa J+a(h+a^{T}c),\qquad\dot{Z}=-\kappa Z+Ma(h+a^{T}Z). (B.3)

These identities prove π⁢D˙=χ⁢H\pi\dot{D}=\chi H directly. Differentiating the symmetric quadratic form in equation (3.36) gives 2⁢π⁢R˙=H22\pi\dot{R}=H^{2}. This is a complete algebraic compatibility check, independent of the unresolved analytic source-contour argument.

Appendix C Fisher–Hartwig normalization calculation#

With g⁢(t)=(2⁢π)−1⁢∫e−i⁢p⁢t⁢log⁡σ⁢(p)⁢dpg(t)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int e^{-ipt}\log\sigma(p)\mathrm{d}p, expand

The cosine integral gives

g⁢(t)=−1π⁢∑n≥11n2+t2=12⁢π⁢t2−coth⁡(π⁢t)2⁢t.g(t)=-\frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{1}{n^{2}+t^{2}}=\frac{1}{2\pi t^{2}}-% \frac{\coth(\pi t)}{2t}. (C.2)

Because t⁢g⁢(t)2∼1/(4⁢t)tg(t)^{2}\sim 1/(4t) at infinity, the quadratic integral requires a logarithmic subtraction. After u=π⁢tu=\pi t, use

∫0∞uz−1⁢(coth⁡u−u−1)2⁢du=22−z⁢Γ⁢(z−1)⁢(z−3)⁢ζ⁢(z−1),−2<ℜ⁡z<0.\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{z-1}(\coth u-u^{-1})^{2}\mathrm{d}u=2^{2-z}\Gamma(z-1)(z-3% )\zeta(z-1),\quad-2<\Re z<0. (C.3)

The strip follows from the quadratic behavior at zero and constant limit at infinity. The finite part of the right-hand side at z=0z=0 is

γE−23+log⁡2+12⁢ζ′⁢(−1).\gamma_{E}-\frac{2}{3}+\log 2+12\zeta^{\prime}(-1). (C.4)

Undoing the factor 1/41/4 and the coordinate change gives CEC_{E} in the main text.

In the single-root Wiener–Hopf/Fisher–Hartwig normalization, with interval length 2⁢Q2Q,

βFH\displaystyle\beta_{\rm FH} =CE−γE4+2⁢log⁡GB⁢(3/2)+14⁢log⁡2\displaystyle=C_{E}-\frac{\gamma_{E}}{4}+2\log G_{B}(3/2)+\frac{1}{4}\log 2
=−16+14⁢log⁡(4⁢π)+3⁢ζ′⁢(−1)+2⁢log⁡GB⁢(3/2).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{4}\log(4\pi)+3\zeta^{\prime}(-1)+2\log G_{% B}(3/2). (C.5)

Here GBG_{B} is Barnes’ function. Its duplication and special-value identities reduce this to equation (5.9). This fixes all constants used in the numerical comparison without fitting.

This calculation is an evaluation within the standard normalization, not a new proof of the general Fisher–Hartwig theorem. A self-contained theorem for this particular symbol should check the limiting regularity and factorization hypotheses after separating its root. The determinant comparison tests the resulting normalization very sensitively but does not replace those hypotheses.

Appendix D Spectral trace and logarithmic Rayleigh correction#

D.1 Evaluation of the trace integral#

The Green-kernel calculation first gives

All required rapidity derivatives reduce to scalar endpoint-length derivatives. Put

Appendix F Interval certification of the reference equation#

Let yj,wjy_{j},w_{j} be exact Gauss–Legendre nodes and weights on [−Q,Q][-Q,Q], enclosed by interval arithmetic. Computed coefficients cjc_{j} are treated as fixed decimal numbers, not as an exact linear-system solution. The analytic trial profile is

fN⁢(x)=g⁢(x)+∑jwj⁢K⁢(x−yj)⁢cj,f_{N}(x)=g(x)+\sum_{j}w_{j}K(x-y_{j})c_{j}, (F.1)

where g=1g=1 or KK. Every node residual fN⁢(yj)−cjf_{N}(y_{j})-c_{j} is interval-evaluated.

For 0<δ<10<\delta<1, the physical ellipse of semiminor axis δ\delta has parameter

ϱδ=δQ+1+(δ/Q)2,kδ=1π⁢(1−δ2).\varrho_{\delta}=\frac{\delta}{Q}+\sqrt{1+(\delta/Q)^{2}},\qquad k_{\delta}=% \frac{1}{\pi(1-\delta^{2})}. (F.2)

For real x∈[−Q,Q]x\in[-Q,Q], its analytic integrand obeys

|K⁢(x−y)⁢fN⁢(y)|≤Mδ=kδ⁢(gδ+kδ⁢∑jwj⁢|cj|),|K(x-y)f_{N}(y)|\leq M_{\delta}=k_{\delta}\left(g_{\delta}+k_{\delta}\sum_{j}w% _{j}|c_{j}|\right), (F.3)

with gδ=1g_{\delta}=1 or kδk_{\delta}. Gauss quadrature is exact through degree 2⁢N−12N-1. Bounding the remaining Chebyshev coefficients gives

|∫−QQK⁢(x−y)⁢fN⁢(y)⁢dy−∑jwj⁢K⁢(x−yj)⁢fN⁢(yj)|≤8⁢Q⁢Mδ⁢ϱδ−2⁢N1−ϱδ−1.\left|\int_{-Q}^{Q}K(x-y)f_{N}(y)\mathrm{d}y-\sum_{j}w_{j}K(x-y_{j})f_{N}(y_{j% })\right|\leq\frac{8QM_{\delta}\varrho_{\delta}^{-2N}}{1-\varrho_{\delta}^{-1}}. (F.4)

Add (2⁢Q/π)⁢maxj⁡|fN⁢(yj)−cj|(2Q/\pi)\max_{j}|f_{N}(y_{j})-c_{j}| for the collocation residual, then use equation (4.2) for the solution enclosure.

The implementation brackets each Legendre root by a disjoint certified sign change and encloses its weight. At Q=0.9Q=0.9, N=64N=64, δ=0.9\delta=0.9, raw bounds are below 2.44×10−472.44\times 10^{-47} for DD and 1.19×10−471.19\times 10^{-47} for RR. Conservative output radii are 10−4610^{-46}. At Q=2Q=2, N=96N=96, the radii are 10−3210^{-32} and 10−3310^{-33}. Computations use mpmath interval arithmetic at at least 110 decimal digits; the code is not separately formalized in a proof assistant.

This certificate is independent of the trans-series. It certifies neither a finite-order Padé continuation nor a Borel-integral tail nor equality of an infinite sector sum with the exact solution.

Appendix G Reproducibility and the evidence ledger#

The archive retains three computational modules with their original internal layouts, preserving the relative paths to coefficient files and quadrature caches.

Directory Contents
reproducibility/endpoint/ Flow generator, seeds, point sectors, primitive blocks, Chebyshev TBA, lateral/Green summation and failed-method scans.
reproducibility/
determinant_thermal/ 		Determinant sectors, parity Nyström reference, gap solver and thermal checks.
reproducibility/

The source hashes identify the September PDF and the supplied inputs. The unpublished O(3) note by Dániel Nógrádi is retained privately and is not included in the public supplementary archive. Archived notes preserve the calculation’s chronology; the present manuscript supersedes their comparisons with the March version.

G.1 Checks and principal resummations#

Install requirements.txt. Run each module’s run_checks.py from its own code directory:

⬇
cd reproducibility/endpoint/code
python run_checks.py
cd ../../determinant_thermal/code
python run_checks.py
cd ../../spectral_reconstruction/code
python run_checks.py

The principal endpoint test uses the supplied coefficients:

⬇
# From reproducibility/endpoint/code
python green_resum.py ../data/sectors200_n12.json \
--Q .9 -T 190 --phi .50 --inner 384 --outer 32 \
--dps 200 --evaldps 90 --out ../results/green_new.json
python factorized_resum.py ../data/basis200_r8.json \
--Q .9 --T0 198 --TI 190 --TF 130 --phi .4 \
--nodes 512 --dps 200 --green ../results/green_new.json \
--out ../results/factorized_new.json

The Green file is specific to QQ, and a mismatched value is rejected. The determinant and interval tests are

⬇
# From reproducibility/determinant_thermal/code
python determinant_numeric.py resum --Q .9 --T 154 \
--phi .45 --nodes 512 --dps 170
# From reproducibility/spectral_reconstruction/code
python interval_tba.py --Q 0.9 --n 64

The optional 210-order seed regeneration uses C++17 and Boost; the commands and numerical precision are specified in the endpoint module’s README. Its output is included, so regeneration is not required for the comparisons.

G.2 Fresh audits and retained production records#

For this manuscript all three test suites, the principal factorized endpoint sum and its Green replacement, the 154-term determinant sum, and the Q=0.9Q=0.9, N=64N=64 interval certificate were rerun. Figure and table data were regenerated from the records. The full high-order flow and every large spectral or thermal scan were not rerun wholesale; their raw outputs and code are retained, with representative checks in the fresh suites.

The archive provides all complex sector contributions, cumulative sums, angle/order scans, eight limiting fractional modes, four finite-QQ gap modes, deformed determinants at several spectral parameters, both thermal ensembles at two densities, and failed conformal tests. Main-text tables select decisive comparisons but expose the unresolved next order. No formal sector beyond the tested levels is described as numerically resolved.
